market_context: United States; food-safety thresholds follow FDA and USDA guidance.
title: How Long Does Food Last in the Refrigerator During a Power Outage?

seo.title: Fridge Without Power: How Long Food Stays Safe
seo.meta_description: An unopened refrigerator keeps food cold for about 4 hours. After that, perishable food needs ice or another cold source; smell and appearance cannot prove it is safe.
seo.search_intent: Know how long refrigerated food can remain safe during a power outage and which foods should be kept cold or discarded.

excerpt: An unopened refrigerator generally keeps food at a safe temperature for about 4 hours. If the outage lasts longer, perishable foods such as meat, seafood, milk, eggs and leftovers need to be kept at 40°F (4°C) or below with ice or another refrigerator; food that has been warm too long should be discarded.
content_html:
About 4 hours is the key refrigerator window during a power outage, provided the door stays closed. FDA and USDA guidance uses that period because an insulated refrigerator warms gradually after the electricity stops. Four hours is not a magic spoilage switch, but beyond it you should no longer assume perishable food has stayed at 40°F (4°C) or below unless you have a thermometer or another reliable cold source.

The most useful first move is to leave the door shut. Opening the refrigerator to check the food releases cold air and shortens the time you have. If the outage is likely to continue, set up a cooler with ice or frozen gel packs before the refrigerator becomes warm.

The four-hour guideline assumes the door is mostly closed

A working refrigerator should keep food at 40°F or colder. Once power stops, insulation slows heat from entering but cannot stop it. How quickly the interior warms depends on room temperature, how full the refrigerator is, how cold it was before the outage and how often the door is opened. The four-hour figure is therefore a conservative food-safety guide rather than an exact prediction for every appliance.

An appliance thermometer makes the decision much easier. If power returns and the refrigerator or food is still at 40°F or below, that temperature information is more useful than guessing from the clock alone. Without a thermometer, a long outage creates more uncertainty, particularly for high-risk perishable foods.

Meat, seafood, dairy, eggs and leftovers deserve the most caution

Foods that normally require continuous refrigeration include raw or cooked meat and poultry, fish and shellfish, milk, yogurt, soft cheese, eggs and egg dishes, cooked leftovers, prepared meals and many cut or cooked foods. If those items spend several hours above safe refrigeration temperature, cooking them later is not a dependable rescue method.

Bacteria can multiply while food warms. In some foods, bacterial toxins can also become a concern, and reheating does not reliably reverse every problem created by poor temperature control. Tasting a bite is not a safety test either. Dangerous foodborne organisms can be present without making food smell sour, look slimy or taste unusual.

Not everything stored in the refrigerator has to be discarded

Hard cheeses, butter, whole uncut fruits and vegetables, many acidic condiments and some shelf-stable products tolerate a temporary loss of refrigeration better than meat or milk. The exact decision depends on the product, whether it has been opened and the manufacturer’s storage directions. Something being stored in the refrigerator does not automatically make it a highly perishable food.

Raw meat juices create a separate issue. If a leaking package contaminates ready-to-eat food while the refrigerator warms, discard the contaminated food rather than trying to rinse it. If you move perishables to a cooler, use enough ice or frozen packs to keep the cooler at 40°F or below; “cool to the touch” is not a measured food-safety temperature.

After power returns, use time and temperature rather than smell

If power was off for no more than about 4 hours and the refrigerator remained closed, refrigerated food is generally within the window described by FDA and USDA. With a longer outage, check a thermometer if one is available and separate truly perishable foods from more stable items. When you cannot verify that high-risk food stayed cold, discarding it is the safer decision.

For future outages, keeping a refrigerator thermometer inside is inexpensive and removes much of the guesswork. Frozen gel packs or bottles of water can also be kept ready for a cooler. If severe weather is expected, freezing meat or leftovers you will not need immediately can buy extra time because frozen mass warms more slowly.

The rule worth remembering is “about 4 hours, door closed.” After that, perishable food needs a dependable source of cold or temperature evidence. A normal smell does not certify safety.

faq.question: Should I open the refrigerator during a power outage?
faq.answer: As little as possible. Every opening releases cold air and shortens the time the refrigerator can stay within a safe temperature range.

faq.question: Can I cook meat that got warm during the outage?
faq.answer: Cooking is not a reliable way to rescue food that has spent too long above safe refrigeration temperatures because bacterial growth or toxins may already be a concern.

faq.question: Can I use smell to decide whether food is safe?
faq.answer: No. Bad odor is a reason to discard food, but dangerous bacteria can be present even when food looks and smells normal.
